thread.subject: Re: RE: made you something
thread.body_text:
Hey Kyle, this is interesting - I definitely like the way it creates a system. I will say, I'm doing a lot of Springs Fireplace writing with my own GPT and I think I could make this playbook more authentic by feeding existing content into it. In addition, I can tell these photos are AI, and I don't love that. All that being said, I would still like to learn how your product works, and I have set up some time for next week. I simply wanted to offer this feedback so you understand my thinking before our call.  

 Thanks, 
 Lauren

this is exactly the kind of feedback I want, thank you Lauren.
 

 you're right that you can tell on the photos, and that one's on the inputs. those mockups were built from whatever I could pull off your site, so the model was guessing at your bottles, your labels, your peppers. when we build creative for a brand we're actually running, we start from their real product photography and shoot library, and the output stops reading as generated. same tools, completely different starting point.
 

 and on the playbook, no argument. yours was written from the outside in, site and reviews only. feeding your own content into it is the right instinct.
 

 the part I'd focus on next week is the layer above the creative, how the account is structured, what gets tested in what order, and how you know which angle is working before you spend real money on it. that's the piece a GPT can't do for you.
 

 see you next week.

 - Kyle

copy.tldr: Springs Fireplace is a premium seed-to-bottle hot sauce brand with a real story and an Oprah's Favorite Things badge, but zero ads running and zero reviews on site, so this call is about starting clean from their best products, not fixing a broken account.

deep_dive.what_they_are: A small-batch condiment brand that grows rare peppers on their own East Hampton farm and with regional partners in NY and NJ. They bottle hot sauces, salsas, and dried chili flakes. They got named to Oprah's Favorite Things 2025, which is a real trust badge worth using.
deep_dive.what_they_sell: 12 products from $8 to $35. Dried chili flakes at $8 (Gochugaru, Espelette, Aleppo, Aji Limon), hot sauces at $14 (Tesuque, Aji Peach, Aji Mango), salsa at $9 (Salsa Roja), a rare pepper at $35 (Charapita), and bundles at $26 to $33 (The Duo, Aji Lovers, The Trifecta). Median price is $14, and I am using that as a stand-in for their average order value since we cannot see their real numbers.
deep_dive.positioning: Premium, provenance-first artisan condiments. The pitch is flavor and heritage over generic store-bought heat. Glass not plastic. Clean ingredients, no added sugar, made to elevate flavor not overpower it.
deep_dive.who_buys: Flavor-curious home cooks and food lovers who care about where things come from and will pay more for a hot sauce with a real story. Not the extreme-heat crowd. People who want everyday flavor with a heritage angle.
strengths: Oprah's Favorite Things 2025 plus two 2025 Scovie/Flave awards. That is strong outside proof we can put right in the ads.
Clear bestseller signal: Tesuque is called out as their best-selling everyday hot sauce and is award-winning, and it anchors both bundles.
gaps: No reviews anywhere on the site. A premium brand with no visible social proof is harder to sell to a cold shopper.
No Meta ads running now, so there is no past data to learn from. We start from zero.

game_plan.headline: Lead with the award-winning bestseller Tesuque and the Oprah badge to prove one ad can sell cold, then widen to bundles and a second hero sauce.

phases.goal: Prove that a cold stranger will buy from one ad. Nothing more. Find the one angle that works.
campaigns: One simple sales campaign, small number of audiences, broad targeting so Meta can find the buyer.
Test the 3 Scroll-Stopper ads we already wrote against each other so we learn which angle wins before spending real money.
lead_products: Tesuque hot sauce ($14). I would lead with this because the site calls it their best-selling everyday condiment and it won a 2025 Scovie Award. It is the safest bet for a cold audience: everyday use, award-backed, and it anchors both the Duo and Trifecta bundles, so a Tesuque buyer has a clear next purchase.
phases.creative: Run the 3 ads from the Scroll-Stopper Sheet first, since this lead was promised a plan built from those ads. Important: rebuild them using Lauren's real product photos, not the mockup images. She already told us she can spot the AI photos and does not like them, so real bottle and label shots are non-negotiable here. Lead the winning angle with the Oprah's Favorite Things badge and the Scovie award. Push the FIRST15 code as the first-order nudge.
phases.what_success_looks_like: We can point to at least one of the three ads that gets cheap clicks and at least a few sales, and we know which angle people respond to. We are not chasing profit yet, we are buying an answer.

phases.goal: Put more money behind the winning ad and angle. Widen who sees it. Start bringing back people who visited but did not buy.
campaigns: Scale the winning Tesuque ad and audience with a slow budget increase.
Add a simple retargeting campaign to people who visited the site or added to cart but did not buy, leading with the Duo bundle to lift order value.
lead_products: The Duo bundle ($26), Tesuque plus Aji Peach, used in retargeting to raise average order value above the single-bottle price.
phases.creative: Make 2 or 3 fresh versions of the winning angle so it does not go stale. Add a customer or founder story angle if Lauren has any real testimonials or a farm-to-bottle video, since that plays to the heritage strength.
phases.budget: Step up toward $100 to $150 a day, only if month one found a winner.
phases.what_success_looks_like: The winning ad holds up at higher spend and retargeting brings back buyers at a lower cost than cold traffic.

phases.goal: Scale what works and add a second hero product so we are not resting on one sauce.
campaigns: Keep scaling the winning Tesuque campaign.
Launch a second product test around Aji Mango, their newest and spiciest sauce that was 'back in stock,' aimed at the fruit-and-fire crowd.
lead_products: Aji Mango ($14) as the second hero. It is their newest sauce and the boldest, which gives us a fresh story to run and a different buyer than Tesuque.
The Trifecta ($33) offered to repeat visitors and past buyers to push order value up.
phases.creative: Separate creative for Aji Mango leaning on tropical-and-fiery and the ceviche/Peruvian chile story. Keep the Oprah badge in the mix.
phases.budget: Scale toward $150 to $250 a day, gated on the return holding.
phases.what_success_looks_like: Two products selling from ads, not one, and a repeatable way to test the next sauce after that.

estimates.label: Starting budget
estimates.basis: enough to get roughly 25 to 40 clicks a day at typical costs for a food brand, which is the floor for learning which of the 3 ads works before spending real money

estimates.label: Average order value stand-in
estimates.basis: the median price across their 12 products, used as a stand-in because we have no access to their Shopify. Real number could be higher if bundles sell well

estimates.label: Revenue we would aim to add
estimates.value: We are not putting a 90 day revenue number on this yet
estimates.basis: with no ad history, no reviews, and a $14 order value, any dollar figure would be a guess. To give an honest target we need their true average order value and their margin, which are in the discovery questions

assumptions: Their real average order value is close to the $14 median. If bundles push it higher, the plan gets easier and budget can move faster.
Lauren can give us real product photography to rebuild the ads. If she cannot, creative slows down.
Margin on a $14 sauce is healthy enough to survive paid ads plus the 15% first-order code. If margin is thin, we rethink the offer.
Checkout and shipping work fine. The shipping policy page reads as empty, so we should confirm shipping is actually set up.

questions.question: Are you spending anything on ads right now, on Meta or anywhere else?
questions.listening_for: We found no Meta ads running. Confirm if that means never tried, or tried and stopped. If they stopped, ask why. That changes everything.

questions.question: Who handles marketing today, you or someone on your team?
questions.listening_for: Lauren said she does a lot of the writing with her own GPT. Find out if she is a solo founder wearing every hat or has help. Tells you how hands-on we need to be.

questions.question: What does a typical order look like, one bottle or do people buy a few things at once?
questions.listening_for: This is the real average order value. We are guessing $14 from the median. If people usually buy bundles, the number is higher and ads work sooner.

questions.question: Roughly what is left after the cost of the product and packing, on a $14 sauce?
questions.listening_for: Margin. A premium glass-bottle product may have real costs. If there is not enough room after the FIRST15 discount, paid ads will struggle. Do not push the plan hard if margin is thin.

questions.question: When people land on your site, do they tend to buy, or do most leave? Any sense of that?
questions.listening_for: If traffic already converts, the problem is just getting eyes on it. If it does not convert, ads will not fix a leaky site and we address that first.

questions.question: Do you have any reviews or customer messages saved anywhere, even in email or DMs?
questions.listening_for: There are zero reviews on the site. This is a real weakness for cold ads. If she has praise sitting in her inbox, we can put it to work fast. If there is none, we need a plan to collect it.

questions.question: Can you give us your real product photos and any video from the farm or kitchen?
questions.listening_for: She already flagged she does not like the AI mockups. Confirm she has a real photo library. This is the single biggest thing that decides if creative moves fast.

questions.question: Which product actually sells the most for you right now?
questions.listening_for: We are betting on Tesuque because the site calls it the bestseller. If she says something else sells more, we lead with that instead. This one answer can change the whole plan.

questions.question: How much of your business comes from your own site versus stores?
questions.listening_for: They have a store locator, so wholesale may be a big part of the business. If most sales are wholesale, online ads matter less and we size expectations down.

questions.question: Are people already searching for things like 'gochugaru,' 'Aleppo pepper,' or 'Espelette' and finding you?
questions.listening_for: These are named peppers people actively look up when cooking a recipe. That is a real search opening. If she has never looked at Google search, there is likely money on the table there.

questions.question: When someone hears about you from the Oprah list or a store, where do they go to find you?
questions.listening_for: If people are typing 'Springs Fireplace' into Google after seeing the brand somewhere, we want to make sure Google is not sending those buyers to a competitor. That is a cheap, easy win.

objections.objection: I do a lot of my own brand writing with my own GPT already.
objections.answer: Good, keep doing that, the words are yours and they should be. The part we handle is above the words: how the account is built, which ad gets tested first, and how you know an angle is working before you spend real money on it. That is the piece the writing tool cannot do for you.

objections.objection: I could tell those photos were AI and I do not love that.
objections.answer: You are right, and that was on the inputs. Those were built from whatever was on your site, so it was guessing at your bottles and labels. When we run a brand for real, we start from your own product photos and video. Same idea, real starting material, and it stops looking generated. If you send us your shoot library, that problem goes away.

objections.objection: We have never really run ads. How do I know this will work for a small hot sauce brand?
objections.answer: We do not assume it works. That is why month one is small, around $50 a day, and its only job is to buy an answer. We run the three ads against each other and see which one a stranger actually buys from. We only spend more once we have proof. You will not be scaling into the dark.

objections.objection: My orders are small, mostly one $8 to $14 bottle. Can ads even pay off on that?
objections.answer: That is the honest risk, and it is why we lead with your $14 bestseller Tesuque and use your Duo and Trifecta bundles to lift order size right away. It is also the number I most need from you, because I am guessing $14 from your prices. Tell me your real average order and your margin and I will tell you straight whether the math works.

red_flags.flag: No reviews anywhere on the site.
red_flags.why_it_matters: Cold shoppers trust other buyers. For a premium price, no social proof makes the first sale harder. We lean on the Oprah and Scovie badges to fill the gap, but we need to start collecting reviews early.

red_flags.flag: Low average order value, likely around $14.
red_flags.why_it_matters: Small orders leave little room to pay for a click and the FIRST15 discount. If margin is thin, paid ads may not clear. Confirm the real order value and margin before promising anything.

red_flags.flag: The shipping policy page appears blank.
red_flags.why_it_matters: If shipping is not clearly set up or is expensive on an $8 bottle, people abandon at checkout. Sending paid traffic to a broken or unclear checkout wastes money. Confirm shipping works before we spend.

red_flags.flag: Several products need refrigeration and some say 'email to get on the list' or 'back in stock.'
red_flags.why_it_matters: We should not scale ads on a product that keeps selling out or has stock limits, like Charapita or Aji Lovers. Lead only with products she can reliably keep in stock.
They have a store locator and are in stores. If most revenue is wholesale, online ad results will look small and we should set expectations accordingly.

other_channel_openings: Google search is a real opening. Their peppers have names people actively look up when cooking, like Gochugaru, Aleppo, Espelette, and Aji Amarillo. People searching those terms have intent to buy. Worth raising once the Meta plan is agreed.

Brand-name search protection. After the Oprah's Favorite Things feature and in-store placement, people will Google 'Springs Fireplace.' A small Google presence makes sure those warm buyers land on their site, not a reseller or competitor.
